newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-British rates unchanged as inflation eases.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-British rates unchanged as inflation eases.

text.p: Britain's Conservative government left interest rates unchanged on Thursday, despite recent pressure from the Bank of England for an increase, as official figures showed annual inflation fell in December.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said retail price inflation slowed to 2.5 percent year-on-year in December from 2.7 percent in November, while the underlying rate, which excludes mortgage interest payments, dipped to 3.1 percent.

"These figures show that subdued cost pressures and a stronger pound are feeding through to lower inflation," Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke said in a statement after the data were released.
Clarke met Bank of England Governor Eddie George on Wednesday for their monthly meeting on monetary policy.

Although no statement was made after the talks, the Bank carried out routine money market operations at established rates on Thursday morning, indicating that official rates remained unchanged at 6.0 percent.
The Bank has repeatedly called for an increase in interest rates in recent months because it fears inflation will head higher this year.
But in a BBC radio interview, Clarke, who has the final say on monetary policy, made clear he was still not convinced that the economy was beginning to overheat.
"When I make decisions on interest rates I look at how good were conditions in shops for Christmas, what is happening to production, how strong is the housing market getting," he said.
"The big thing at the moment is the pound is very strong and that is very anti-inflationary."

December retail sales appear to have been weaker than expected, while figures already released show manufacturing output actually fell last month. The strong pound dampens inflation by making imported goods cheaper for British firms.

The chancellor has a strong political incentive to avoid raising interest rates in the run-up to an election, which is due by May, as higher rates mean more expensive home loans for millions of Britons.

City economists said Clarke may have to concede an interest rate increase at the next monetary meeting on February 5 if fourth-quarter gross domestic product (GDP) data due in the meantime showed the economy growing strongly.

However, some believe he might be tempted to "tough it out" and keep interest rates unchanged right through to the election in an effort to narrow the strong lead which the opposition Labour party enjoys in opinion polls.

"Although the odds are probably still in favour of a pre-election rise in interest rates, these numbers, along with the strength of the pound, suggest that there is a chance that Mr Clarke can hold off altogether," said Jonathan Loynes, an economist at HSBC Markets.
The ONS said retail prices rose 0.3 percent last month, after a 0.1 percent rise in November. The fall in the annual rate to 2.5 percent was largely due to motoring costs and food prices.
Economists said inflation should decline further in the coming months, but the government will have difficulty in meeting its target of 2.5 percent underlying inflation by the end of this parliament.
